THIS CHAPTER IN 60 SECONDS
  • Inclusive growth (World Bank): both the pace and the pattern of growth, addressed together. The Indian model: Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas.
  • Eight components (the teacher's star diagram): economic, social, institutional, financial, technological, gender, geographic, political inclusion. The chapter repeats this same eight-fold list for need → challenges → measures → way forward.
  • Trickle-down vs inclusive: trickle-down assumes growth plus redistribution reaches everyone; inclusive growth makes people active contributors through jobs and capabilities.
  • Bharatiya Model of Inclusive Development: three pillars: Indic market economics, Antyodaya and empowerment, holistic approach.
  • Financial inclusion: five pillars on a base of digital public infrastructure and digital identity; PMJDY, Stand-Up India, MUDRA, SVANidhi and UPI; RBI FI Index 64.2 → 67.0.
Understand it firstThink of growth as a feast. Trickle-down hopes crumbs fall from the top table. Inclusive growth seats everyone at the table and teaches them to cook: jobs, skills, services, accounts. Financial inclusion is giving each guest a plate (an account), a fork (credit) and a napkin (insurance). This picture is a memory aid, not from the handout.
WORDS YOU NEED FIRST
WordPlain meaning (aid: verify before quoting)
Inclusive growthGrowth whose pace and pattern both bring benefits to all groups, not only a few.
Trickle-downIdea that growth at the top reaches the poor later through jobs and spending.
Antyodaya"Rise of the last person": caring for the most disadvantaged first.
Indic market economicsThe teacher's phrase for a balanced mix of private enterprise and market forces with selective government intervention (a "middle path").
Financial inclusionAffordable, accessible banking, credit, insurance and pension for all.
FI IndexRBI's Financial Inclusion Index (access, usage, quality).
First-cycle borrowerSomeone taking a loan for the first time (MUDRA).
Account AggregatorA framework that lets a person share verified bank and GST data with lenders, with consent.
Digital divideGap between people who can and cannot use digital services.
RememberOne line to carry: Inclusion has eight faces; every question on this chapter can be answered by walking the same eight faces: need, challenge, measure, way forward.

1 · INCLUSIVE GROWTH: CONCEPT, DATA AND SALIENT FEATURES
PYQ 2022 · 10m · is inclusive growth possible under a market economy? Significance of financial inclusionPYQ 2014 · 12.5m · capitalism and inclusive growthHandout pp.83-84 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstGrowth can be like a fast bus that many people miss. Inclusive growth asks: how fast is the bus (pace) and who gets a seat (pattern)? The World Bank says both must be solved together. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Introduction: according to the World Bank, inclusive growth refers both to the pace and pattern of growth, which are interlinked and must be addressed together.
  • Indian model of inclusive growth: Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas.

2 · TRICKLE-DOWN VERSUS INCLUSIVE GROWTH
PYQ 2014 · 12.5m · capitalism and inclusive growth (your file)Handout p.85 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstTrickle-down: the government backs growth at the top (the tip of the pyramid), collects more tax, then redistributes. Inclusive model: start at the bottom and build jobs and capabilities so that people themselves drive development. Memory aid, not from the handout.
Trickle-down (teacher's triangle)
Government focus of growth (top of the pyramid)
High growth → more tax revenue
Redistribution back down
Issues: assumptions of trickle-down (teacher)
1The sector of choice grows at pace
2Government can collect more tax
3Government chooses to redistribute, not reinvest
4Efficiency of redistribution
  • The government focuses on capital owners (capitalism-based growth); others are passive recipients.
Inclusive growth model (teacher)
Make people active contributors to the development process
At the bottom of the pyramid → jobs and capabilities
Jobs → opportunities → industrial development
Capabilities → skill development (capacities rise)

3 · NEED FOR INCLUSIVE GROWTH (EIGHT FACES)
PYQ 2016 · 12.5m · challenges of inclusive growth including careless and useless manpower; measuresHandout p.86 (teacher's handwriting)
FaceNeed (teacher)Evidence given
1 Economic inclusionTranslate output growth into stable jobs and reduce regional disparities.Large regional disparities in HDI (Goa vs Bihar) and per capita income; majority of workers in informal jobs.
2 Social inclusionEquitable access to health, education and nutrition (human resource → human capital).Public service deficit: ~2% of GDP on health and 4.6% on education; NFHS-5: stunting 35.5%, wasting 7.7%, underweight children 32.1%.
3 Institutional inclusionStrong, accountable institutions to deliver basic services, enforce standards and reduce informality.Prevalence of informality in the labour market.
4 Financial inclusionAffordable and accessible finance ensuring consumption, investment in skills and formalisation of livelihoods.Existence of digital finance divide; low employability due to skill mismatch → difficulty in getting formal credit.
5 Technological inclusionNew growth drivers (tech, FDI, GVC) must benefit a large population.Digital access limits constrain uptake of e-services.
6 Gender inclusionFundamental to household welfare and aggregate productivity.Persistent disparity: poor performance in Gender Inequality Index.
7 Geographic inclusionBuild resilient local economies and reduce distress migration.Prevailing rural-urban divide in infrastructure, services and opportunities.
8 Political inclusionEnsure resource-use efficiency and effectiveness.Lack of participatory planning and accountability in allocation on health, education, skilling, etc.

4 · CHALLENGES ASSOCIATED WITH INCLUSIVE GROWTH (EIGHT FACES)
PYQ 2016 · 12.5m · challenges and measures (your file)Handout p.87 (teacher's handwriting)
FaceChallenges (teacher)
1 EconomicPoverty and inequality: multidimensional poverty and income inequality prevent economic participation · over-dependence on agriculture: disguised unemployment
2 SocialSystemic marginalisation based on religion, gender, caste or region limits access to nutrition, education and employment (e.g. exclusion of transgender persons from economic activities)
3 InstitutionalCorruption, inefficiency and maladministration misappropriating resources meant for the poor · stringent labour laws restricting formal employment growth
4 FinancialAccessibility to affordable credit for a large section of the population and financial literacy · regional variations in availability of banking services
5 TechnologicalSkill mismatch due to poor industry-academia linkage · lack of digital literacy and internet access in rural areas · siloed government services leading to accessibility issues
6 GenderLow FLFPR (34.7%, PLFS 2024) · societal norms limiting access to good education and jobs · workplace discrimination (glass ceiling, discriminatory recruitment)
7 GeographicRegional disparity in industrial development · accessibility issues leading to development deficit (e.g. North Eastern states) · climate change and disasters hurting tribals, coastal communities, etc.
8 PoliticalGovernance failures leading to trust deficit · discrimination on lines of religion and language

6 · BHARATIYA MODEL OF INCLUSIVE DEVELOPMENT
Handout p.89 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstThe Bharatiya model says India need not copy either extreme: not a command economy, not pure capitalism. Three pillars: enterprise-led growth (Indic market economics), care for the last person (Antyodaya) and evidence-driven pragmatism (holistic approach). Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Introduction: grounded in India's cultural-historical roots, emphasising an indigenous approach to development; includes the significance of family and community in economic and social roles; focuses on sustained, fast and inclusive growth.
PillarWhat it means (teacher)Examples
Indic market economicsBalanced interplay between private enterprise and market forces with selective government intervention · Middle-path approach between a communist-socialist command-and-control economy and an ultra-capitalist one · aims to create a competitive economy, stimulate innovation and ensure inclusive growthPublic Private Partnership · NGOs · Digital Public Infrastructure
Antyodaya and empowermentCaring for and reaching out to the most disadvantaged while providing equal opportunity for all · India's welfare vision blends compassion with capabilityDBT through JAM trinity · PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana · Ayushman Bharat · PM Awas Yojana
Holistic approachIntegrates social welfare and economic growth, focusing on indicators like multidimensional poverty, FLFPR · Pragmatism balances growth, inclusion and sustainability, adjusting policies as per lived realities, data and feedback loopPM Gati Shakti · Aspirational Districts · High capex-driven growth strategy
NoteConclusion for BMID (teacher's pink box): the Bharatiya Model of Inclusive Development fuses enterprise-led growth, Antyodaya-based welfare and evidence-driven pragmatism to achieve sustained, fast and inclusive growth.

9 · FINANCIAL INCLUSION
PYQ 2026 · 10m · financial inclusion as part of social and economic inclusion; usefulness of RBI's FI IndexPYQ 2016 · 12.5m · PMJDY and the institutional finance foldPYQ 2022 · 10m · significance of financial inclusionHandout pp.92-94 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstFinancial inclusion means every household can save, send money, borrow and insure safely. The temple diagram shows five pillars standing on a base of digital identity and digital public infrastructure: take the base away and the pillars fall. Memory aid, not from the handout.
Pillar (handout diagram)Content
Accessibility of financial servicesAccess to bank account · financial services · digital financial services
Availability of varied financial servicesPayments (transfers) · credit · savings · insurance · pension
Affordability of financial servicesLow-interest loans · insurance at an affordable premium
Adequacy of normsCyber protection · adequate rules and regulations · tailor-made services
Awareness of financial servicesFinancial literacy · ICT campaigns
BaseDigital Public Infrastructure and Digital Identity
MNEMONICA-A-A-A-AFive pillars all begin with A: Accessibility · Availability · Affordability · Adequacy of norms · Awareness. Say it: "Five A's hold up financial inclusion." (own memory aid; same order as the diagram)
Progress
  • Adult bank account ownership rose from 35% (2011) to 89% (2021).
  • PMJDY accounts: 55.02 crore by March 2025.
  • RBI Financial Inclusion Index rose from 64.2 (March 2024) to 67.0 (March 2025).
  • Regulatory innovation (digital infrastructure) + government-led microfinance initiatives → increased scale and depth of financial inclusion.
Measures to promote financial inclusion
  • PMJDY: establishing foundational savings and transaction infrastructure for previously unbanked populations; women accessed 69% of all microloans.
  • Stand-Up India: bank loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore to SC, ST and women entrepreneurs for greenfield enterprises.
  • PM Mudra Yojana (PMMY): finances micro and small enterprises in manufacturing, trading, services and allied agricultural activities.
PMMY tier (teacher's infographic)Loan size
Shishuup to ₹50,000: initial capital for micro-start-ups
Kishore₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh: businesses looking to expand
Tarun₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh: mature small businesses needing higher capital
Tarun Plus (NEW)₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh: repeat borrowers with strong repayment records
PMMY trends and impacts (teacher)Detail
Borrower cyclesIn 2023 almost all were first-cycle borrowers. Now: first cycle 51.5% remain, second cycle 32.3%, third cycle 16.1%.
Income2023 to 2025: average annual business income among SVANidhi borrowers up by 20%; borrowers who invested in fixed assets saw faster income growth.
BeneficiariesOne-third are women, 45% OBCs, 17% SCs, 2% STs.
Maturing borrower baseShare of Shishu accounts declined 92% → 63% while Kishore and Tarun expanded; average ticket sizes increased (2x for Shishu, over 7 lakh for Tarun).
Impact assessment by ISBClear progression through loan cycles; formal credit access expanded; NPA rate below 10%.
Welfare effectsBuilding household resilience: housing upgrade, better food access, affordable healthcare, enhanced educational opportunities.
  • PM Street Vendor's AtmaNirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi): collateral-free working capital loans to street vendors.

UPI and financial deepening
  • UPI is publicly provided, interoperable infrastructure: (1) supports inclusion at scale; (2) aligns technological change with macro-level financial development. It is a general-purpose payment instrument and a platform for inclusive growth.
  • Account Aggregator framework (a key DPI pillar): supplies lenders with verified data linking bank transactions and GST records, enabling lending to underserved and first-time credit users.
  • UPI and financial deepening: verifiable transaction histories + reducing transaction costs → bridge the gap in account ownership and access to formal credit; role in reaching new-to-credit borrowers; growth in credit linked to digital payments did not come at the cost of higher default rates.
  • Issues of access friction remain: shows a digital divide rather than resistance to the system itself.
  • Impact: RBI's Financial Inclusion Index rose from 64.2 (March 2024) to 67.0 (March 2025).
Virtuous cycle of financial inclusion (handout infographic)
Secure formal credit access
Practise consistent repayment discipline
Fuel sustainable enterprise growth
Drive rising credit demand (and back to access)

PYQ 2025 · 10m · Inclusive growthDistinguish between the Human Development Index (HDI) and the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI) with special reference to India. Why is the IHDI considered a better indicator of inclusive growth?★ Write: Handout hook only: HDI disparity (Goa vs Bihar), multidimensional poverty, Gini 25.5 (World Bank).Where / gap: Gap: IHDI itself is not in this handout.
PYQ 2026 · 10m · Financial inclusionExamine the view that financial inclusion is an integral part of social and economic inclusion in a country like India. Also throw light on the usefulness of the R.B.I.'s Financial Inclusion Index.★ Write: Integral: financial inclusion is one of the eight inclusions; needed for consumption, skills, formalisation. Pillars (5 A's), PMJDY, Stand-Up India, MUDRA, SVANidhi. FI Index: 64.2 → 67.0 (March 2024 to March 2025); measures access, usage, quality; shows effect of regulatory innovation and microfinance.Where / gap: Section 9
PYQ 2021 · 15m · Inclusive growth"Investment in infrastructure is essential for more rapid and inclusive economic growth." Discuss in the light of India's experience.★ Write: Handout hook: geographic inclusion: PM Gram Sadak Yojana, Bharatmala / Sagarmala, Bharat Net, Border Area Development; digital public infrastructure for financial and technological inclusion; NITI Aayog and WEF: investment in labour-intensive infrastructure, water, electricity.Where / gap: Sections 5, 7, 8
PYQ 2022 · 10m · Inclusive growthIs inclusive growth possible under market economy? State the significance of financial inclusion in achieving economic growth in India.★ Write: Market economy: Indic market economics (private enterprise + selective state role), PPP, DPI; trickle-down limits. Financial inclusion: virtuous cycle (secure credit → repayment discipline → enterprise growth → rising credit demand), MUDRA progression, UPI and Account Aggregator, FI Index 67.0.Where / gap: Sections 2, 6 and 9
PYQ 2016 · 12.5m · Inclusive growthComment on the challenges for inclusive growth which include careless and useless manpower in the Indian context. Suggest measures to be taken for facing these challenges.★ Write: Challenges (section 4): skill mismatch from poor industry-academia link, informality, disguised unemployment, low FLFPR, digital divide. Measures: skilling (NEP, Skill India Mission, SkillFuture-type credits), MSME push, MUDRA, labour law modernisation, apprenticeship, PM Vishwakarma.Where / gap: Sections 4, 5 and 8
PYQ 2014 · 12.5m · Inclusive growthCapitalism has guided the world economy to unprecedented prosperity. However, it often encourages shortsightedness and contributes to wide disparities between the rich and the poor. In this light, would it be correct to believe and adopt capitalism driving inclusive growth in India? Discuss.★ Write: Against pure capitalism: trickle-down assumptions (sector grows, tax collected, redistribution chosen and efficient) often fail; government then focuses on capital owners and others become passive recipients. The Indian answer: Bharatiya model: middle path, Antyodaya, pragmatism with feedback loop; DBT through JAM, PMGKAY, Ayushman Bharat.Where / gap: Sections 2 and 6

TRAPS AND EXAM-HALL RULES
TrapWhy it fools youExam-hall rule
Eight faces versus nine features.The nine salient features (equitable opportunity ... good governance) are a different list from the eight inclusions (economic ... political).Name the list before you start.
FLFPR figures.41.7% (p.83, PLFS 2023-24) and 34.7% (p.88, PLFS 2024) both appear.Quote one with year and source.
"Middle path" means socialism.The teacher's Bharatiya model is a middle path between command-socialist and ultra-capitalist economies.Write "between the two extremes".
Stand-Up India versus MUDRA.Stand-Up India: ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore, SC/ST/women, greenfield. MUDRA: up to ₹20 lakh (Tarun Plus).Keep the sizes apart.
FI Index is a rate.It is an index score (64.2 → 67.0), not a percentage.Write "index points".
SkillFuture is Indian.It is Singapore's initiative; the Indian best practices are Rythu Bandhu and Amma Canteen.Keep the two columns separate.

SELF-TEST (answer key below)
  • Q1. How many inclusions does the teacher's star diagram show? (a) 5 (b) 6 (c) 8 (d) 9
  • Q2. Rythu Bandhu gives: (a) ₹5,000 per acre per season (b) ₹10,000 per farmer (c) free fertiliser (d) 5% interest subvention
  • Q3. Which is a pillar of financial inclusion in the diagram? (a) Adequacy of norms (b) Aggregation (c) Autonomy (d) Agency
  • Q4. Tarun Plus loan range: (a) up to ₹50,000 (b) ₹5-10 lakh (c) ₹10-20 lakh (d) ₹20-50 lakh
  • Q5. RBI FI Index in March 2025: (a) 64.2 (b) 67.0 (c) 55.02 (d) 89
  • Q6. Brazil's conditional cash transfer is: (a) Bolsa Familia (b) Oportunidades (c) SkillFuture (d) Amma
  • Q7. Which belongs to the Antyodaya pillar? (a) PM Gati Shakti (b) PPP (c) PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (d) DPI
NoteAnswer key: Q1 c (Economic to political; nine is the number of salient features.) · Q2 a (Benefits ~5.8 million farmers.) · Q3 a (Five A's: accessibility, availability, affordability, adequacy, awareness.) · Q4 c (New tier for repeat borrowers.) · Q5 b (64.2 was March 2024.) · Q6 a (Oportunidades is Mexico's.) · Q7 c (PPP and DPI are Indic market economics; Gati Shakti is holistic.)

ABBREVIATION COLUMN
Abbreviation columnEvery short form in this chapter, with its full form and a one-line plain meaning. The meanings are plain-language aids to help revision: verify them before quoting in an answer.

ACPS: Aadhaar Cheque Payment System (as read; verify). payment system on teacher page 88

AI: Artificial Intelligence. computer systems that do tasks needing human-like learning or judgement

BMID: Bharatiya Model of Inclusive Development. the teacher's three-pillar model

CAA: Constitutional Amendment Act. as in 73rd, 74th and 106th CAA

CMIE: Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy. private think-tank that publishes monthly unemployment data

CPGRAMS: Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System. online portal for citizen grievances

CSR: Corporate Social Responsibility. company spending on social causes; the handout links internship reporting to CSR-style disclosure

DBT: Direct Benefit Transfer. money sent straight to a beneficiary's bank account, cutting leakage

DPI: Digital Public Infrastructure. shared digital systems (ID, payments, data) that many services can build on

FDI: Foreign Direct Investment. long-term investment by a foreign firm in a business in another country

FI: Financial Inclusion. access to affordable financial services for all

FLFPR: Female Labour Force Participation Rate. share of working-age women who are working or looking for work

GDP: Gross Domestic Product. value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year

GST: Goods and Services Tax. India's indirect tax on goods and services

GVC: Global Value Chain. a product made in stages across several countries

HDI: Human Development Index. UNDP index of health, education and income

ICDS: Integrated Child Development Services. nutrition and early-care scheme for children and mothers

ICT: Information and Communication Technology. computers, internet and digital tools; taught as an employability skill

IHDI: Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index. HDI reduced for inequality

ISB: Indian School of Business. institute that did the MUDRA impact study

JAM: Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile. trinity used for direct benefit transfer

KISAN: PM-KISAN. income support to farmers, listed under Part C

MGNREGA: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act. 100-day wage employment law for rural households

MSME: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. small firms by investment and turnover limits

MUDRA: Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency. agency behind collateral-free micro loans (PMMY)

NEP: National Education Policy. 2020 education reform policy

NITI: National Institution for Transforming India. government think tank (NITI Aayog)

NPA: Non-Performing Asset. a bank loan that has stopped being repaid

NRLM: National Rural Livelihoods Mission. mission that promotes SHGs

NULM: National Urban Livelihoods Mission. urban poor skilling and self-employment mission

OBC: Other Backward Classes. socially and educationally backward groups

PDS: Public Distribution System. subsidised foodgrains through ration shops

PLFS: Periodic Labour Force Survey. NSO survey that measures employment and unemployment (LFPR, WPR, UR)

PM: Prime Minister. head of the Union government

PMGKAY: Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana. free foodgrain scheme

PMJAY: Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana. ₹5 lakh health cover

PMJDY: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana. zero-balance bank account scheme for the unbanked

PMMY: Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana. loans to micro and small enterprises in Shishu, Kishore, Tarun, Tarun Plus tiers

POSHAN: POSHAN 2.0. nutrition mission for children, adolescents and mothers

PPP: Public-Private Partnership. project shared between government and private firm

PRI: Panchayati Raj Institution. rural local self-government

PSL: Priority Sector Lending. bank lending targets for priority sectors

RBI: Reserve Bank of India. India's central bank

RTE: Right to Education. free and compulsory education law (Art. 21A)

RTI: Right to Information. law to get information from public bodies

SC: Scheduled Castes. constitutionally listed castes with reservations

SHG: Self-Help Group. small group of women that saves and borrows together

SHRI: PM Schools for Rising India (PM SHRI). central school-upgrading scheme listed under Part B

ST: Scheduled Tribes. constitutionally listed tribes with reservations

SWAYAM: Study Webs of Active-Learning for Young Aspiring Minds. government platform for free online courses; SWAYAM Plus adds industry-aligned ones

UID: Unique Identification. the Aadhaar number system

ULB: Urban Local Body. municipality or city local government

UPI: Unified Payments Interface. instant mobile payment system

WEF: World Economic Forum. global think-tank that publishes growth and inclusion reports
